stem: Which situation matches the lecture definition of a robot kinematic singularity?

options.text: Every matrix describing the robot becomes symmetric
The robot changes its coordinate labels
A nonzero vector changes length
The Jacobian loses rank

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 7: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: The determinant is a scalar calculated from a square matrix; it indicates invertibility and acts as a scaling factor for linear transformations. Rank is the maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns. A^-1 exists if det(A)≠0 and AA^-1=I; A^-1=adj(A)/det(A). Loss of Jacobian rank is a singularity; the slide writes det(J)=0.

solution.justification: Singularity concerns lost independent directions, not merely large or small numerical entries.

optionExplanations.o1: This removes an independent velocity-mapping direction; the slide connects it to failure of inversion.
optionExplanations.o2: Symmetry is unrelated to the rank-loss definition.
optionExplanations.o3: Renaming coordinates alone is not a rank loss.
optionExplanations.o4: Scaling alone need not make a mapping singular.

solution.simpleExplanation: Singularity concerns lost independent directions, not merely large or small numerical entries.

stem: Why does the definition explicitly exclude x=0 from being an eigenvector?

options.text: A0 is undefined
Zero vectors have infinite norm
All eigenvalues must be nonzero
A0=lambda 0 holds for every lambda and cannot identify an eigen-direction

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 8: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: For square A, an eigenvector x is nonzero and satisfies Ax=lambda x. The characteristic equation is det(lambda I-A)=0. Eigenvectors/eigenvalues represent principal directions and scaling factors. The slide states asymptotic stability when real parts of all system-matrix eigenvalues are negative.

solution.justification: The equation is informative only when the vector supplies a genuine direction.

optionExplanations.o1: The zero vector supplies no direction and would make the equation vacuous.
optionExplanations.o2: Any finite matrix can multiply the compatible zero vector.
optionExplanations.o4: A singular square matrix can have a zero eigenvalue with a nonzero eigenvector.

solution.simpleExplanation: The equation is informative only when the vector supplies a genuine direction.

stem: Which expression is the mean of a continuous variable with density f_X?
subtopic: PMF versus PDF and continuous expectation
tags: PMF versus PDF and continuous expectation

options.text: Integral over realx of x f_X(x) dx
Integral over realx of f_X(x) dx
The largest value of f_X(x)
Sum of all valuesx without probability weighting

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 13: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: A random variable is a function X:Omega→R mapping experimental outcomes to real numbers. Discrete mean E(X)=sum_i x_i P(X=x_i); continuous mean E(X)=integral from -infinity to infinity of x f_X(x) dx. Discrete variables use PMFs; continuous variables use PDFs. Expected robot reward is a probability-weighted average.

solution.justification: The factorx changes normalization into an average value.

optionExplanations.o1: The slide weights each continuous value by its density and integrates.
optionExplanations.o2: For a normalized PDF this is 1, not the mean.
optionExplanations.o3: A peak density is not a mean.
optionExplanations.o4: This ignores the probability law and is not the displayed expectation.

solution.simpleExplanation: The factorx changes normalization into an average value.

stem: What makes the displayed grasping decision tree interpretable?

options.text: Its output is chosen randomly after every observation
It guarantees every object is physically safe under every circumstance
Its sequence of explicit tests and outcomes explains the selected force
It has no intermediate conditions

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 24: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Information gain=H(Parent)-sum_child P(Child)H(Child); choose the attribute with largest entropy reduction. The grasping diagram tests Surface=Glass? Yes→Fragile→Low Force. No→Thickness? Thick→High Force; Thin→Low Force. Explicit logic supports safety, interpretability and control.

solution.justification: A person can trace why a particular low/high-force decision was reached.

optionExplanations.o1: The path can be traced from observed attributes to the action.
optionExplanations.o2: It visibly contains surface and thickness tests.
optionExplanations.o3: The figure shows deterministic rules for the listed inputs.
optionExplanations.o4: The pedagogical rule does not establish such a universal engineering guarantee.

solution.simpleExplanation: A person can trace why a particular low/high-force decision was reached.

options.text: The probability of success decreases to 0 with more time
The probability of finding a solution tends to 1 as time tends to infinity
Every finite run is certain to find a solution
Every found path is necessarily the shortest

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 27: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Completeness concerns finding a solution if one exists. The slide distinguishes complete, resolution complete (fine enough discretization), and probabilistically complete (success probability tends to 1 as time tends to infinity). It says genetic algorithms may find near-optimal paths but do not guarantee the absolute shortest path in finitely many steps. Unqualified claims about A* and genetic algorithms require assumptions.

solution.justification: Asymptotic success probability does not supply a fixed deadline for guaranteed success.

optionExplanations.o1: This is the limit statement in the slide.
optionExplanations.o2: A limiting probability is not certainty at each finite time.
optionExplanations.o3: The property concerns finding a solution, not its optimality.

solution.simpleExplanation: Asymptotic success probability does not supply a fixed deadline for guaranteed success.
misconceptions: Reading an infinite-time limit as a finite-time promise.
examTraps: Reading an infinite-time limit as a finite-time promise.

stem: Which pairing matches the lecture summary?

options.text: Probability/statistics: perception and decisions under uncertainty
Graph search: replacing every rigid-body inertia tensor
Big-O notation: directly computing a robot end-effector pose
State-space models: counting transitive verbs in independent sentences

citations.locator: Lecture 3 printed slide 28: relevant definition/equation and any named figure; visual transcription normalized to plain-text notation
citations.evidenceText: Summary associates linear algebra with kinematics/dynamics/control; calculus with motion/velocity/dynamics; probability/statistics with uncertainty; state-space models with control; graph search with navigation; complexity/completeness with algorithm selection. SVD and chain rule are named here but not developed in this lecture.

solution.justification: Choose mathematical tools by the kind of problem: uncertainty, geometry, dynamics, search, or scaling.

optionExplanations.o1: This is the role stated in the summary.
optionExplanations.o2: Graph search concerns navigation/decision structure, not inertia representation.
optionExplanations.o3: Complexity evaluates algorithm scaling, not a geometric pose.
optionExplanations.o4: That is the distribution example, not the state-space role.

solution.simpleExplanation: Choose mathematical tools by the kind of problem: uncertainty, geometry, dynamics, search, or scaling.
